source: Xi, Cheng, Soni, Turner (2026) Evaluating Creative Generative AI with Conceptual Blending (EvalEval @ ACL 2026 position poster)
finding: Gap 1 closed as negative. The poster is a position paper. It proposes to score LLM outputs on FrameNet frame blends (1,000+ frames, 10,000+ lexical units) with a six-item rubric. It does not label outputs as simplex, mirror, single-scope or double-scope, and it reports no scores.
numbers: No numbers reported. Rubric items: Completeness, Clarity, Relevance, Understanding Depth, Coherence, Execution Time. Example blend: Giving_birth with Success_or_failure.
quote: Creativity is not random novelty, but the ability to generate outputs that integrate distinct conceptual domains
limits: A one-page poster, a proposal not an experiment. Understanding Depth and Coherence target everyday (Mini-C, Little-C) creativity only. Inter-rater reliability is listed as future work.
agent_relevance: Confirms nobody has yet scored LLM output by network type. A usable rubric idea: score cross-frame output on integration depth and coherence, not on novelty alone.

source: Fauconnier and Turner (1998; expanded web version 2001) Conceptual Integration Networks, Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187
finding: Gap 2 part 1. The 1998 paper does not use the words simplex, mirror, single-scope or double-scope (zero hits in the full text). It uses an older typology: frame networks (all spaces share one organizing frame), one-sided networks (inputs have different organizing frames and the blend extends only one), and two-sided networks (different frames, and some topology comes from both). The four-way names appear in the 2002 book and the 2003 paper.
numbers: Worked examples: Regatta, Debate with Kant, Buddhist monk = frame networks. Boxing business competitors (Murdoch knocked Iacocca out) = one-sided. Computer desktop, 'digging your own grave', complex numbers, same-sex marriage = two-sided.
quote: A shared topology network is one-sided if the inputs have different organizing frames and one of them is projected to organize the blend.
limits: Read in the expanded 2001 web version, not the journal print. The 2002 book chapter was not opened. Mapping old to new names (frame = mirror, one-sided = single-scope, two-sided = double-scope) is our reading.
agent_relevance: Gives an operational test the agent could apply: which organizing frame structures the output, and do roles from both frames appear in it.

source: Fauconnier and Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks, section on two-sided networks and optimality
finding: Gap 2 part 2: which type suits novelty. The authors say two-sided networks give more chance of non-optimal blends and of conflict between optimality principles, but also the opportunity for creativity. Their worked discovery is complex numbers: multiplication comes from the number frame, angle from the geometry frame, and running the blend shows multiplication adds angles, an unexpected property.
numbers: No quantitative data. Examples only: complex numbers, desktop interface; Fourier, Maxwell, Faraday named as further cases.
quote: The fact that in two-sided networks the organizing frame of the blend is not available by extension from the organizing frame of either input increases chances of non-optimality
limits: The creativity claim is argued from historical cases chosen after the fact. There is no comparison with one-sided or frame blends that were not creative.
agent_relevance: Supports a design rule with a cost: cross-frame (double-scope) combination raises both the chance of a novel result and the chance of a bad one, so a check must follow it.

source: Fauconnier and Turner (2003) Conceptual blending, form and meaning, Recherches en Communication 19:57-86
finding: Gap 2 part 3. Gives the four network types in one paragraph. Simplex: one input is a frame, the other holds specific elements. Mirror: one organizing frame is shared by all spaces. Single-scope: input frames differ and the blend inherits only one. Double-scope: essential frame and identity properties come from both inputs, which can resolve clashes. The four are prototypes on a continuum, not exclusive boxes.
numbers: No numbers. Examples: 'buying gasoline' frame (simplex); 'He threw the ball over the fence' as a role-value mapping in a simplex network; 'dolphin-safe', 'shark-safe', 'child-safe' as successive double-scope blends.
quote: In Double-Scopes, essential frame and identity properties are brought in from both inputs.
limits: Short definition in an overview; the 2002 book chapter has fuller treatment and was not opened. The typology is stated as a continuum, so hard labels are a simplification.
agent_relevance: The agent can label planned steps with a type but should treat the label as a soft score, not a hard class. Closes most of the secondary-source weakness in K01.

source: Fauconnier and Turner (2003) Conceptual blending, form and meaning, claims on creativity
finding: Gap 2 part 4. The authors tie double-scope blending to creativity and to human uniqueness: 'a powerful source of human creativity' and 'universal for our species'. They offer no test. Their examples of double-scope products are everyday (a tuna can label, causative grammar), not only inventions, so double-scope is not rare.
quote: Double-Scope Blending can resolve clashes between inputs that differ fundamentally in content and topology. This is a powerful source of human creativity.
limits: Theoretical claim. Same authors as the typology, so not independent support for 'double-scope for novel ideas'.
agent_relevance: Our design hypothesis (use double-scope for novel ideas) has its origin here and stays untested. The authors also say double-scope is common, so it may be cheap to run.

source: Peng et al. (2025) Probing and Inducing Combinational Creativity in Vision-Language Models, Figure 5 re-read from the PDF image
finding: Gap 4 closed. I rendered Figure 5 and read the bars. Fusion precision is higher than replacement precision for 9 of the 11 models (and for average people). Replacement is higher only for Claude-3.5-Sonnet and LLaVA-1.6-13B. The body text is right; the Figure 5 caption ('consistently higher precision for replacement') is a wording error.
numbers: Approximate bar values read from the chart: GPT-4o replacement 0.74 vs fusion 0.78; MiniCPM 0.56 vs 0.67; LLaVA-1.5-7B 0.39 vs 0.53; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 0.62 vs 0.59; LLaVA-1.6-13B 0.65 vs 0.57; Qwen-VL-Chat 0.54 vs 0.55; average people 0.52 vs 0.54.
quote: Analysis of 11 models reveals higher precision metrics for fusion combinations in 9 models
limits: Values read by eye from a bar chart. No significance test is reported for fusion vs replacement. Task is identification of input objects in images.
agent_relevance: Fusion (both inputs visible) is easier to decode than replacement (one input dominant). Balanced blends are easier to take apart than one-sided ones. Resolves K10.

source: Hernandez et al. (2024) Alien Recombination: Exploring Concept Blends Beyond Human Cognitive Availability in Visual Art
finding: Gap 9 closed. 'Alien' pairs are concept combinations that are unlikely both in existing artworks (Art model, GPT-2 fine-tuned on WikiArt concepts) and in any single artist's concept set (Cognitive Availability model, also GPT-2). Candidates are ranked by weighted rank aggregation of the two perplexities, then rendered with DALL-E. Raising temperature is not enough: it yields combinations new to the artworks but not ones unavailable to artists. Novelty was judged by GPT-4 pairwise and by ResNet152 embedding distance.
numbers: 50 input sequences (1 or 2 concepts); 150 outputs per input per temperature; temperatures 0.1 to 3.1 in steps of 0.3. Above temperature 1, 85% of combinations contain at least one concept new to the artworks. At temperature 3 more than half still have N_cog = 0 (nothing unavailable to artists). Image test used alien weight 0.85. Exact GPT-4 win rates are in a figure only.
quote: cognitive unavailability is a promising metric for optimizing artistic novelty, outperforming mere temperature scaling
limits: Art domain, WordNet Core vocabulary, small GPT-2 models. GPT-4 judge and ResNet embeddings both partly measure visual factors. No human raters. A text-domain equivalent is plausible: rank candidate pairs by how rarely the two concepts co-occur, then keep coherent ones.
agent_relevance: A code-side ranker for far pairs: sample many candidate pairings, rank by low co-occurrence plus coherence, keep the top. Fits the Kombine finding that default blends are familiar and homogeneous (K11).

source: Kombine (2025) Table 10 blending full scores, human sample, sampling temperature (re-read from PDF text)
finding: Gap 7 partly closed. The paper does not publish the share of blends at Q=1, Q=2 and Q=3. It publishes one column, 'Emerg. integ.', as percent of the maximum, per model. All models were sampled at one temperature (0.9, top-p and top-k off), so no temperature effect can be read. Model size is not controlled, but the ranking is steep: top models score high and small ones low.
numbers: Emerg. integ. (percent of max): gpt-5.6-sol 76.7, gpt-6-astra 65.0, gemini-3.7-flash 60.0, claude-fable-5 56.7, gemini-3.1-pro 55.0, claude-opus-4.6 41.7, deepseek-chat 26.7, llama-4-maverick 11.7, gpt-4o-mini 8.3, phi-4 3.3, humans 1.3. Utility (valid blend) gpt-5.6-sol 83.3 vs humans 12.8. Humans: 120 recruited, N=75 kept. 35 LLMs.
quote: All models are sampled at temperature T = 0.9 with top-p and top-k parameters disabled
limits: Values are zeroed when a blend fails utility, so integration quality is mixed with validity. A percent of max does not give the Q=1/2/3 split. Model names are as printed in the paper. LLM-judge panel; human agreement 75% on unanimous items. Single temperature.
agent_relevance: Nothing here says how often an LLM reaches the double-scope-emergent level. Measure it ourselves with a code check on shared slots. Humans scored far lower, so human baselines are not a ceiling for this task.

source: Kombine (2025) definitions of blend quality Q and the limitations section
finding: Gap 5 answered as negative. Kombine defines Q=1 (single-scope) when projected structure comes from both inputs, Q=2 (double-scope) when both inputs also fill at least one shared slot, Q=3 (double-scope emergent) when an emergent property also appears, citing Fauconnier and Turner (2008). Its generic-space check is made by an LLM judge. No experiment adds a code-side verify-shared-slot gate or any self-check before blending, and the limitations section does not propose one.
numbers: Only comparisons: valid generic space 43.4%, coherent blend given a valid space 97.1%. Judge prompts tag each triple as u, v, uv (shared slot) or emergent.
quote: separate "u" and "v" lines that never share a slot are a concatenation, not a fusion
limits: The Kombine scale is not the 2003 typology: in F&T 2003 a single-scope blend inherits ONE frame, here single-scope means both inputs contribute. Do not cite Kombine as a test of F&T types. The judge prompt shows the shared-slot test could be turned into a check.
agent_relevance: The gate is untested but cheap: have the model name the shared slot and one fact per input that fills it, verify both facts separately, then build the blend. Predicted gain is the 43.4% to 97.1% gap.

source: Mizrahi, Shani, Stanovsky, Jurafsky, Shahaf (2025) Cooking Up Creativity: Enhancing LLM Creativity through Structured Recombination (Dish COVER)
finding: Gap 3 (text-only). A pipeline where the LLM only parses and writes, and ordinary code does the combining (tree edit-distance blend of two recipe trees, value filter, novelty ranking). In human ratings by Prolific raters with cooking experience it beat a prompt-tuned GPT-4o on novelty, with value about equal. The blend step is done by code, which is the code-side blend idea.
numbers: Exp 1 (10 dish pairs, 50 recipes per model): novelty 3.53 vs 3.146 (p=0.0009); valuable 80% vs 82%, value 4.320 vs 4.326. Exp 2 (100 recipes per model): novelty 3.612 vs 3.141 (p=9.2e-8); valuable 85% vs 98%, value 4.36 vs 4.51. Dish COVER made up 75.55% of the top novelty quartile. 48 raters, 5 ratings per recipe, Krippendorff alpha 0.201 and 0.209. Nearest-corpus similarity 0.774 vs 0.851. Temperature up to 1 used; above 1 GPT-4o gave gibberish.
quote: significantly surpass GPT-4o in terms of novelty and diversity
limits: Cooking only. Raters agree poorly (alpha about 0.2). The GPT-4o baseline got 104 and 114 paraphrased prompts with experts picking the best single prompt, but it is a single call, not equal compute. Value was lower for Dish COVER in Exp 2 (85% vs 98%).
agent_relevance: First text-only evidence that moving the combine step out of the model into explicit code raises novelty at about equal value. Needs a reasoning-task version. It costs value: add a validity gate.

source: Mizrahi et al. (2025) Dish COVER, qualitative analysis of GPT-4o 'shallow merges'
finding: Gap 3 and gap 9. By default GPT-4o juxtaposes rather than integrates: for two dishes it prepares each separately and joins them at the end (burger between two waffles; muffins baked plus orange salad served beside). This is a concatenation, the failure Kombine labels. Outputs are also homogeneous.
numbers: GPT-4o recipes had 24.98 ingredients (SD 5.2) and 465.84 words in Exp 1 vs Dish COVER 12.3 and 240.28; self-BLEU-2 0.929 (Exp 1) and 0.912 (Exp 2); same-pair cosine similarity 0.90; mean tree distance 89.35 vs 132.14 (p=3.6e-5). Mean pairwise embedding similarity 0.659 vs 0.387 (Exp 1), 0.731 vs 0.402 (Exp 2).
limits: Qualitative judgment by the authors on one model (gpt-4o-2024-08-06). The longer GPT-4o output confounds the comparison.
agent_relevance: Add an output check: if the answer can be split back into input A and input B without loss, it is a juxtaposition and must be redone as a fused version.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners, ICLR 2024
finding: Gap 3 (text-only reasoning). Asking the model to recall or invent relevant problems and knowledge before solving beat 0-shot and few-shot chain of thought on math, code and BIG-Bench. This is analogy recall, not blending: nothing in it fuses two frames.
numbers: Average accuracy gain +4% across tasks and base models (GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, PaLM2). Codeforces and MATH gains are the most notable. BIG-Bench with GPT-3.5-turbo (0-shot CoT / 3-shot CoT / ours): temporal sequences 40.4 / 44.8 / about 58; colored objects 50.4 / 61.6 / about 62 to 68 (table text garbled, two 'ours' rows). Works better with larger models; with small models retrieved CoT is better.
quote: outperforms 0-shot CoT and few-shot CoT across a range of tasks and base LLMs, achieving an average accuracy gain of +4%
limits: The extra generated exemplars add tokens, so it is not equal-token. The GSM8K table could not be cleanly read from the PDF text. It does not test any 'how the inputs combine' step.
agent_relevance: Shows a pre-answer generation step helps text-only reasoning, but only for analogy recall. A blend-specific text-only reasoning test is still missing.

source: Palamas (2025) Making the Familiar Unfamiliar: AI-Driven Synectics Metaphor Generation for Computational Creativity (ICCC 2025)
finding: Gap 3 and gap 6 (closest thing to varying the kind of cross-frame link). GPT-4 was asked for four Synectics analogy types per theme (Direct, Personal, Symbolic, Fantasy). The more distant type gave higher creativity and lower coherence. This is a type manipulation, but not the Fauconnier and Turner types, and it was judged by GPT-4 and TF-IDF, not people.
numbers: 1,000 GPT-4 metaphors (100 per theme, ten themes, temperature 0.9) vs 1,000 human metaphors. Fantasy: creativity 4.8, coherence 3.8. Direct: coherence 4.5, novelty 3.9. Theme creativity: Dreams 4.8, Knowledge 4.7, Hope 4.7, Power 4.3, Love 4.2. AI metaphors more novel but less coherent than human ones; creativity comparable.
quote: Fantasy analogies scored highest in creativity (4.8) but lowest in coherence (3.8)
limits: GPT-4 scored its own output (self-preference risk). Novelty is TF-IDF distance. No human raters; preliminary results. No test of whether the metaphors work.
agent_relevance: Gives direction for the distance dial: a more distant frame raises novelty and cuts coherence. Use a coherence check after distant combinations.

source: Eppe et al. (2018) A computational framework for conceptual blending, Artificial Intelligence 256:105-129
finding: Gap 8 part 1. The COINVENT/Cobble system searches generalisations of two input theories, checks consistency, and scores each blend with three metrics tied to the optimality principles. The paper states it has no empirical evaluation. Only worked examples in mathematics and music are shown.
numbers: Score: value(c) = infoValue(c) + compression(c) - imbalance(c) if c is consistent, else 0. Imbalance is half the absolute difference of information taken from the two inputs. No benchmark numbers.
quote: it is by no means close to a solid empirical evaluation
limits: Authors say half of the imbalance (instead of the full difference) 'turned out to be more useful' but give no data. Weights were not tuned. Domain: formal theories only.
agent_relevance: A ready code-side score for ranking blends: reward kept input content and shared structure, penalise one-sided use, zero for inconsistent. The imbalance term is a rough proxy for 'both frames contribute' (double-scope). It could be tested on the agent's own blends.

source: Lieto and Pozzato (2020) A description logic framework for commonsense conceptual combination integrating typicality, probabilities and cognitive heuristics (arXiv 1811.02366)
finding: Gap 8 part 2. A logic framework (TCL) that combines two concepts (e.g. pet and fish) by choosing a head concept and a modifier and resolving property conflicts with probabilities. It reports worked examples with scenario probabilities, not scores against human data or any benchmark.
numbers: Example outputs: scenario probabilities such as 28.22%, 12.10%, 7.06% in blocks; no accuracy or human-agreement figure found in the text.
limits: Concept combination (head-modifier) is closer to a simplex or single-scope pattern than to full blending. Only the arXiv text was read; the journal version may add evaluation.
agent_relevance: Head-modifier selection with conflict resolution is a possible rule for single-scope steps. No baseline numbers exist to borrow.

source: Birdsell (2019) Creative Cognition: Conceptual Blending and Expansion in a Generative Exemplar Task, IAFOR J. Psychology and Behavioral Sciences 5(SI)
finding: Gap 6. A human creativity study that applies blending theory to products, but does not code network types or relate them to novelty scores. 25 usable student drawings of an alien creature were mostly structured by known animals. Five were analysed qualitatively as blends. The text says creativity typically uses double-scope networks, citing F&T 2002, without testing it.
numbers: 34 students asked, 25 completed responses. Legs 72%, eyes 88%. Just over half resembled an earth animal; 20% idiosyncratic (balloon, dust particle, chocolate bar, parasol).
quote: Creativity typically utilizes the mental operation of conceptual blending called double-scope networks
limits: Small class sample, five hand-picked responses, no raters, no control. Cannot support any claim about network type and novelty.
agent_relevance: Replicates the Ward structured-imagination finding: most 'novel' ideas stay near known frames. A far-frame step is needed to leave them. Gap 6 stays open.
